account.ask-for-sign.p1: Settings → Account → Ask for a sign-in (on the page and in the Android app) switches the sign-in on or off. An install that had an account before v1.1.8 keeps asking until you switch it off. Off, anything on your home network or on your own Tailscale network comes straight in (with the built-in Tailscale, only your own devices on it: not one shared in from someone else's tailnet, nor an address your internet provider gives from the same range): a TV showing the shelf or the wall needs nothing typed. Each browser and app is still a device of its own, listed in Settings → Account. From anywhere else (a port forwarded to the internet) a sign-in is still needed, and with no account there is none to give. Switching it on with no account asks you to create the account first; devices already in stay in until you sign them out.
account.ask-for-sign.p2: With the sign-in off, a device comes in without one only when it asks for the server by a name used at home — its address, a bare name, or one ending .local, .lan, .home.arpa or .ts.net — so another web site can't reach it through a name of its own. Anything but a read must come from Mandarin's own page or the Android app: a page of another site open in a browser at home can't restart the server, change a setting or restore a backup. A device let in without a password works only from home and your tailnet, never from the internet.
account.ask-for-sign.p3: Behind a reverse proxy (an nginx, Caddy or tailscale serve on the same machine, or one elsewhere on your network), name it in TRUSTED_PROXIES (TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1 for one on the same machine) and have it say who asked (X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP or Forwarded). Mandarin believes only the proxies named and its own built-in Tailscale: a request that names a caller through anything else, or a named proxy that names nobody, is taken as the internet, never home, and the log says so.
account.ask-for-sign.title: Ask for a sign-in
account.forgot-password.p1: On Mandarin OS, type passwordreset at its own screen (a keyboard plugged in), then yes. Installed on Linux, run on the server:
account.forgot-password.p2: It removes the account and signs every device out; your library, edits and history stay. Then create the account again from a device at home.
account.forgot-password.title: Forgot the password?
account.lead: One account, kept on the server itself — nothing online — or, if you'd rather, none.
account.top.li1: Open http://<server-ip>:3500 on a device on your home network (a browser, the iPhone home-screen app, or the Android app) and choose a username and password, or tap Use without an account.
account.top.li2: With an account, every other device signs in with it once and is remembered.
account.top.li3: Settings → Account lists every device, with a Sign out button for each, and changes the password.
account.your-password-stays.p1: The password never crosses the network, even on plain http: devices prove they know it with SRP (the scheme Apple uses for HomeKit pairing), and the server proves it knows the account back. The server stores only an SRP verifier, never the password.
account.your-password-stays.p2: Five wrong passwords from one address in 15 minutes lock it out for 15 minutes (for IPv6, its whole /64), and guesses sent all at once count as they arrive, so no more than five are ever tried.
account.your-password-stays.p3: Sonos speakers can't sign in: the addresses they're given carry a signature, and the speakers' own addresses are let through, so playback is unaffected.
account.your-password-stays.title: Your password stays yours
apps.lead: The same interface everywhere, because it comes from the server.
apps.top.fine1: ⬇ Get it from Downloads
apps.top.fine2: Sideload it on Android 8.0 or newer; it updates itself from then on, from Settings → Updates. Installed before v0.6.10? Those builds used a different signing key, so Android refuses the update. Uninstall once, install the download and sign in again; downloaded albums need downloading again. Updates install in place after that.
apps.top.fine3: A native app (Kotlin and Jetpack Compose), in android/. The download, mandarin-android.apk, is the newest build, published by GitHub Actions on every version merged to main; the build itself is named Mandarin-Android-<version>.apk, and the link keeps one name so it always points at the newest. Building the app yourself? Without the MUSICD_KEYSTORE_BASE64 and MUSICD_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD secrets, a build is signed with the shared key committed in the repository (android/app/musicd-debug.keystore) and named …-shared-key.apk. It can't update the published app, nor the published app it.
apps.top.p1: Enter the port (3500 unless you changed it) and it finds the server on your Wi-Fi by itself, or type the address; then sign in, create the account on a new server, or use it without one. On top of the interface it adds lock-screen and notification controls, volume keys, a now-playing widget, a Quick Settings tile, a share sheet, Android Auto, This phone as a room, downloads, a USB DAC driver, and Tailscale for away from home.
apps.top.p2: Open http://<server-ip>:3500 in Safari, tap Share → Add to Home Screen. It opens full screen like an app, with the same interface as the Android app.
apps.top.p3: Out of the house, the Android app keeps playing over mobile data: see Away from home. The app's own features are on Features.
away.away-only-phone.note1: For a server with no one at it, give it an auth key instead, as the server's TS_AUTHKEY (see Settings for the server). Don't advertise your home subnet from the server's Tailscale: requests through a subnet router arrive from a home address, and the server can't tell they're away.
away.away-only-phone.p1: Whatever reaches the server from outside your home network — Tailscale included — is offered one room: the phone asking, as This phone. The Sonos rooms aren't listed, and nothing away can play to them, pause, group or mute them, or reach another phone. The server decides this by where each request comes from, so it holds for any device: an iPhone or a laptop on Tailscale can browse the library but has nothing to play to. At home everything is as before.
away.away-only-phone.p2: Away, tracks stream as Opus 256 kbps by default (about a quarter of a CD-quality FLAC's data), made through a 64-bit float resample to Opus's 48 kHz and decoded on the phone by the app's own libopus; Settings → Setup → Downloads → Stream as in the app can send the original files instead. Albums you've downloaded play from the phone. On a weak signal the track that's playing comes first: the tracks after it are fetched only once it has enough.
away.away-only-phone.p3: At home the app keeps its own Tailscale running only while the phone is playing, so walking out of the house doesn't stop the music; back home, the phone plays from home again, and the engine stops as soon as the app is off screen or the phone stops playing. The engine also stops itself when nothing goes through it (two and a half minutes, with the app neither on screen nor playing) or when it is busy for nothing (a fifth of a core for a minute, with nothing passing through), so Android has no cause to end the app for it. It starts again in seconds when the app is used or you leave, its sign-in kept on the phone.
away.away-only-phone.p4: The server's Tailscale keeps its identity in the data folder, so an update or a reinstall is the same machine. TAILSCALE=off leaves it out; TS_HOSTNAME names it something other than musicd. Tailscale installed on the host still works as before (the server uses its own first when both are there, or TAILSCALE_ADDRESS to say which).
away.away-only-phone.title: Away, only the phone plays
away.lead: Leave the house and the Android app keeps working over mobile data. No ports are opened on your router: the phone reaches the server over Tailscale, a private network between your own devices.
away.set-up-once.li1: On the server, open Settings → Setup → Away from home and tap Sign in to Tailscale. Sign in on Tailscale's page (a free account is enough). The server joins your tailnet by itself as musicd.
away.set-up-once.li2: On the phone, sign Mandarin's app in to the same account: Settings → Setup → Away from home → This phone. The app carries its own Tailscale too — no Tailscale app needed.
away.set-up-once.li3: Open Mandarin once at home: the app learns the server's tailnet address.
away.set-up-once.p1: From then on the app follows the phone's network: on your Wi-Fi it uses the server's home address; on mobile data it goes over its own Tailscale, and the page, the queue and the music carry on without a reload.
away.set-up-once.p2: Anything else signed in to your tailnet — an iPhone with the Tailscale app, a laptop — opens the address Away from home shows.
away.set-up-once.title: Set up once — Tailscale is built in
away.use-tailscale-not.p1: Mandarin speaks plain http, as a server at home has no certificate: safe at home, and over Tailscale, whose own link is encrypted. A port forwarded on your router is neither — what the app sends, its sign-in included, would cross the internet unencrypted. The server's log says so whenever a plain-http request arrives from outside your home network.
away.use-tailscale-not.title: Use Tailscale, not a port forward
bridges.its-log-mandarin.p1: Every Bridge keeps its own log, always, and the server gathers each one's new lines every five minutes into its own Logs, through the same privacy filter. Download all logs (Settings → Setup → Logs, in a browser) has them with every other log, in time order, and the Android app's Save log (Settings → Setup → Logging) has every Bridge's log after the server's, each under its name. See Logs.
bridges.its-log-mandarin.title: Its log, in Mandarin's
bridges.lead: Mandarin's own player for a USB DAC: a device with the DAC on its USB port becomes a room Mandarin plays to, bit-perfect. On Android, on Linux, and as a Raspberry Pi image.
bridges.proving-it-bit.p1: On an Android Bridge, SQ-tool records exactly what its USB driver feeds the DAC and compares it with the file, sample by sample. Mandarin Bridge for Linux and the Raspberry Pi can't be recorded yet.
bridges.proving-it-bit.title: Proving it bit-perfect
bridges.set-up-android.li1: Install Mandarin Bridge from Downloads. Installing needs Install unknown apps allowed for the browser or file manager you open it with.
bridges.set-up-android.li2: Open Mandarin Bridge once. It starts, finds Mandarin on the network, and keeps running.
bridges.set-up-android.li3: Plug the DAC into the USB port. Android asks once whether the app may use it; tick always.
bridges.set-up-android.li4: Optional, under Keep awake: turn off battery optimisation, and keep it starting when the device starts.
bridges.set-up-android.li5: In Mandarin, Settings → Audio Devices: the Bridge is listed by its name; switch it on. There is nothing to tick: the rates, depths and DSD come from the DAC itself. Pick it as the speaker and play.
bridges.set-up-android.p1: Volume. A DAC with a volume control of its own is driven by Mandarin's slider. A DAC without one — a line-out DAC into an amplifier — is on Fixed volume: full level, bit-perfect, the amplifier's knob for the volume.
bridges.set-up-android.title: Set up on Android (a FiiO R7)
bridges.set-up-linux.p1: As root, on the computer the DAC is plugged into:
bridges.set-up-linux.p2: It installs the Bridge and the audio engine, ffmpeg where it isn't there, and a service that starts it at boot. Then switch it on in Mandarin's Settings → Audio Devices. Its page, http://<the computer>:49494/, shows the DAC it plays to (and a choice where more than one is plugged in), what plays and how the DAC is fed, its name on the network, and how DSD goes. On the computer Mandarin runs on, it is how a USB DAC there is played: the server opens no sound device of its own on Linux. On Mandarin OS, choose Mandarin Bridge as it installs, or Install it from the system page's Settings tab.
bridges.set-up-linux.p3: Native DSD, and the kernel. On Linux, native DSD is the kernel's to offer: its USB audio driver lists a DAC's native DSD only where its own list knows the DAC's maker, and any other DAC is given DSD as DoP, even where it takes DSD natively (as Mandarin Bridge for Android plays it). The Bridge reads the DAC's own USB descriptor, and where it says native DSD and the kernel offers none, its page and its log give the one line that has the kernel offer it, for that DAC alone, such as:
bridges.set-up-linux.p4: (with your DAC's own vid and pid, as the page gives them); then unplug the DAC and plug it in again, or restart. To undo it, delete the file and replug.
bridges.set-up-linux.title: Set up on Linux
bridges.set-up-raspberry.li2: Flash it with Raspberry Pi Imager: Choose OS → Use custom. Set your Wi-Fi there if you like.
bridges.set-up-raspberry.li3: Plug the DAC into the Pi's USB port and power it on.
bridges.set-up-raspberry.li4: Its page is at http://mandarin-bridge.local:49494/. With no network set, the Pi opens its own Wi-Fi, Mandarin Bridge Setup (password mandarin-setup): join it from a phone, open http://10.42.0.1:49494/, choose your home network and give its password.
bridges.set-up-raspberry.li5: In Mandarin, Settings → Audio Devices: switch the Bridge on. It plays like any room.
bridges.set-up-raspberry.title: Set up on a Raspberry Pi
bridges.top.p1: Made for a FiiO R7 feeding a small DAC over USB. Mandarin's own USB driver claims the DAC from Android and feeds it at each track's own rate and depth, DSD natively or as DoP: no mixer, no resampling. It keeps the device awake while it plays.
bridges.top.p2: A 64-bit Debian, Ubuntu or Raspberry Pi OS computer beside the DAC, playing with Mandarin's own audio engine. One line installs it; it starts at boot. Its page is at http://<the computer>:49494/.
bridges.top.p3: Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit) with the Bridge in it, for a Pi 3, 4, 5 or Zero 2 W: flash it, plug in the DAC, power on.
bridges.top.p4: ⬇ Get Mandarin Bridge v0.3.10
bridges.top.p5: Updated: over SlimProto, Mandarin now sends Mandarin Bridge a continuous stream of PCM (DSD still goes as DSD).
bridges.top.p6: It finds Mandarin on the network by itself (SlimProto, port 3483; a Linux one can be pointed at it with --server), and Mandarin reads the DAC whole from it (every rate, depth and DSD multiple, nothing to tick); Now playing's signal path says what it feeds the DAC, in its own words. On Mandarin OS, choose it as Mandarin OS installs, or Install it from the system page's Settings tab.
bridges.top.p7: A Bridge that was a UPnP renderer before v0.3.0 keeps the name and settings Mandarin had for it; one whose app is installed again is the device it was.
bridges.updates.figcaption1: Settings → Updates in the Android app: the server, the app and the FiiO R7's Bridge, each with its version and its own button.
bridges.updates.li1: Linux and the Raspberry Pi: in a few seconds, by itself. One that fails as it starts is let go, and the one installed runs on.
bridges.updates.li2: Android: a notification on the device; its tap downloads the update in the browser, and Android's installer asks you to install it. The Bridge holds no permission to install apps itself.
bridges.updates.li3: An Android Bridge from before v0.2.1, or a Linux or Raspberry Pi Bridge from before v0.3.1, needs one last update by hand, from Downloads.
bridges.updates.p1: Every Bridge Mandarin knows has a row of its own on Settings → Updates, its name and version, and its own Check for update, as the server's and the app's: it looks for a newer build now and becomes Update available when there is one. A tap asks the Bridge to update: on Linux and the Pi it fetches the build from GitHub, checks it against the checksum published with it, and puts it in place.

configuration.lead: All optional; set any as an environment variable of the server (installed on Linux: sudo systemctl edit mandarin, then Environment=NAME=value under [Service]). Mandarin OS sets what it needs itself, with no shell to change them in. Everything else is in the app's Settings and kept in the data folder.
configuration.top.p1: The FanArt.tv key (artist photos), the waveform, Smart Picks, the wall display and the Home rows are set in the app's Settings and saved in the data folder.
configuration.top.td1: The web interface, the API, and where speakers fetch audio.
configuration.top.td10: How often the music folders are re-checked in full (only changed files are re-read). Between those, an album copied in or deleted is noticed as it happens: through the file system's own notifications, and on a network share or FUSE folder (SMB, NFS, mergerfs), whose changes made elsewhere aren't told, by looking at its folders every 30 seconds. A deletion shows a few seconds after it; a long copy is read at least every 30 seconds while it goes on, so albums appear one by one. Rescan any time from the menu.
configuration.top.td11: Disk kept for converted tracks. An upsampled track is several times a CD-rate one: with upsampling on, 16 is a better number.
configuration.top.td12: How many tracks are converted at once.
configuration.top.td14: Processor cores kept for playback alone: one, or two while DSP is in use. 1 or 2 fixes the number; 0 shares every core. Settings → Library Scanner → Processor shows the split.
configuration.top.td15: The first music folder, until you change the list in Settings → Music Folders (the Linux installer sets it from --music).
configuration.top.td16: Reverse proxies whose word on who asked is believed (addresses or ranges, comma-separated): 127.0.0.1 for an nginx, Caddy or tailscale serve on the same machine. The built-in Tailscale needs nothing here.
configuration.top.td17: Sign the server's built-in Tailscale in with an auth key instead of from Settings → Setup → Away from home.
configuration.top.td19: The server's name on your tailnet.
configuration.top.td2: Your time zone — Album of the day changes over at 00:01 and Smart Picks at local midnight.
configuration.top.td21: off leaves the built-in Tailscale out (Tailscale on the host still works).
configuration.top.td22: The Python 3 (with numpy) that runs SQ-tool.
configuration.top.td24: The server's address away from home, if the one found on the host's tailscale0 isn't the one to use — an IP, a MagicDNS name, or a full https:// address. See Away from home.
configuration.top.td25: Another MusicBrainz web service (a mirror) for the identification scan, release days and an album write-up's year.
configuration.top.td27: 0 leaves the identification scan out entirely.
configuration.top.td29: Where the MusicBrainz pack is kept (Settings → Library Scanner); overrides the folder chosen there.
configuration.top.td3: A speaker's IP (comma-separated for several), for when multicast discovery is unreliable. One is enough.
configuration.top.td30: The Apple store the identification scan's iTunes lookups use (GB, DE…).
configuration.top.td31: Where AutoEq's results are read from for headphone profiles (Settings → Audio Devices → a device → DSP).
configuration.top.td32: A Last.fm API key for similar artists and albums on album and artist pages, until one is saved in Settings → Setup → API Keys (which then wins). Scrobbling also needs the key's shared secret, saved there.
configuration.top.td4: Hosts on your own network a picture may be fetched from (comma-separated names or IPs): a radio station's logo served at home, say. Mandarin never fetches a picture from its own machine or your network otherwise; the Sonos speakers' own addresses are always allowed.
configuration.top.td5: UPnP/DLNA renderers to ask by address (an IP, or a description URL like http://192.168.1.50:49152/description.xml), for when multicast discovery misses them.
configuration.top.td7: The address speakers fetch audio from. Auto picks the machine's LAN address, skipping VPN, container and VM interfaces, and searches for speakers on every LAN interface. Set it to pin one.

features.account.what: One username and password kept on the server, or none: a TV showing the shelf or the wall needs nothing typed. The password itself is never sent.
features.album.how: Tap any album. Play Now and Queue are on the page; ⋯ has Play Next, Shuffle, Radio, Listen later, Share card, Make this the main version, Edit album and (in the Android app) Download. On a phone, Tracks, Credits, About and Versions are tabs, held at the top as the page scrolls; Versions lists each version with its edition and rate, a tap showing it in place. Versions are told by MusicBrainz's release group, else one act and title with its version words off; a list shows the main one with 2 versions under it. On a computer, swipe sideways or press ← → for the previous or next album. The track playing has a small disc turning beside its number. A classical album is set out as its works and movements, its composers and performers in its head. On a computer, a TV or a tablet held sideways the page fills the screen in three columns, in the browser and in the Android app on a tablet: the cover, its credits and more by the artist on the left; About this album and about its artist in the middle, with Read more; the tracks on the right.

features.aotd.how: Nothing to set up: it sits beside Random Album on Home, with its own switch in Settings → Setup → Home Screen. 00:01 is in the server's time zone.

features.aotd.what: One album you haven't played in a year or more (or never), the same on every device, chosen by the server at 00:01 and kept all day.
features.artist.how: Tap an artist's name on an album's page, on the Artists wall or in Search. Their picture, genres, Play and Shuffle are on top; See all on Overview opens Discography. Who they are is the act your albums are by: its MusicBrainz ID from your files or matches, else the act MusicBrainz lists for your album titles, never just the first of the name. Facts come from MusicBrainz, Wikidata and Wikipedia, pictures from FanArt.tv (with a key), Wikidata or Deezer, similar artists and albums from Last.fm (with a key) or Deezer; the page has no links out to the web. A member's page shows their bands' albums from their years in them; a tap on a member, a band or a similar artist opens theirs. Tap a genre for its albums.

features.artist.what: In tabs, as an album's page: Overview (their albums, similar artists, similar albums you have), Discography and About (biography, members or bands). One artist however a sleeve credits them.
features.artists.how: On a phone or tablet, tap Artists in the row at the foot of the screen. Sort is at the top right; Search in the row finds an artist by part of the name. Tap one for their page. Two acts of the same name (Airbag from Norway, Airbag from Argentina) are told apart by the MusicBrainz artist ID in their files' tags (as Picard writes it), else by Mandarin's own MusicBrainz matches (Settings → Library Scanner), each with its own page, picture and a word to tell them apart.

features.artists.what: Every act as a round picture with their name and album count, sorted A to Z, by most albums or at random. Two acts of one name are two artists.

features.backup.how: Open Settings → Backup & restore, tick what to include, then Back up to the server (or, in the app, Back up to a file on this phone). To restore, pick a backup (or the file), tick the parts and tap Restore. Mandarin keeps a backup of how things were first, then restarts. What a backup holds. The API keys part (and the whole database) holds your Discogs, FanArt.tv and Last.fm keys and the Last.fm sign-in, the Qobuz and Tidal sign-ins (tokens, never a password) and the server's Tailscale identity. Without a passphrase they are in the file as they are, so keep the file as you would keep them. Type a passphrase (8 characters or more) before backing up and they are sealed (AES-256-GCM; v0.9.0): restoring them asks for it, and nothing opens them without it. Everything else in a sealed backup restores without it. A backup never holds your password or other devices' sign-ins.

features.bridge.info: How to set up and use Mandarin Bridge
features.bridge.title: Mandarin Bridge
features.bridge.what: A USB DAC on an Android device, a Linux computer or a Raspberry Pi, as a room Mandarin plays to: over SlimProto, a continuous stream of PCM.
features.credits.how: Nothing to set up: the server looks albums up in the background, a second at a time. Eight show at first; More for the rest. Tap a name for their artist page.
features.credits.info: How to set up and use Album credits
features.credits.title: Album credits
features.credits.what: Under an album's tracks: who played, sang, wrote and made it, each with their parts and the tracks they are on, from the files' tags and MusicBrainz.
features.devices.how: Open Settings → Audio Devices and tap a device. The name you give it is what the speaker list and Now playing show. Output is on a renderer's page. Hide / unhide takes devices you don't use off the list; tap it again and tick one under Hidden to bring it back.
features.devices.info: How to set up and use Audio Devices
features.devices.title: Audio Devices
features.devices.what: Every room, renderer and phone with the rates, depths and formats it takes, your own name for it, and a switch. Renderers play Original or upsampled ×2, ×4 or Max.
features.downloads.how: On an album, ⋯ → Download to this phone. Quality, the download folder, Wi-Fi only and automatic downloads are in Settings → Setup → Downloads in the app.
features.downloads.info: How to set up and use Downloads
features.downloads.title: Downloads
features.downloads.what: Albums kept on the phone as the original files or Opus 256, played without the server. Smart Picks, the Album of the day and new albums can download by themselves.
features.dsd.how: On a device's page in Settings → Audio Devices, switch the DSD rates it takes on or off; Output → PCM as DSD and Modulator make PCM DSD. On Linux, a Mandarin Bridge's own page says when the computer's kernel holds back a DAC's native DSD, and the line that frees it.
features.dsd.info: How to set up and use DSD
features.dsd.title: DSD
features.dsd.what: A device that takes DSD is sent the DSF or DFF itself, natively or as DoP; PCM can be made DSD64–256 with a choice of three modulators.
features.dsp.how: Open Settings → Audio Devices, tap a renderer or the phone, and switch on DSP. Room correction takes one WAV, one for each rate, or a zip of them. Sonos rooms have no DSP here.
features.dsp.info: How to set up and use DSP
features.dsp.title: DSP
features.dsp.what: A parametric EQ of up to ten bands per renderer or phone, headphone profiles from AutoEq, and room correction from an impulse response (a WAV from REW or Dirac).
features.edit.how: On an album, tap ⋯ → Edit album.
features.edit.info: How to set up and use Edit album
features.edit.title: Edit album
features.edit.what: Correct an album's title, artist or year and choose its cover. Edits are kept in the server's database; your music files are not changed.
features.favourites.how: Tap the heart on an album's page. Tap the Favourites row's title for all of them.
features.favourites.info: How to set up and use Favourites
features.favourites.title: Favourites
features.favourites.what: A heart on every album. Hearted albums gather on a Home row.
features.folder-albums.info: How to set up and use One album per folder
features.folder-albums.title: One album per folder
features.folder-albums.what: Each folder is one album. Disc folders inside it, such as Disc 1 or CD2, make one album shown disc by disc, with a two-disc symbol on its cover.
features.folders.how: Open Settings → Music Folders and add a folder from the list of drives and folders the server can see. Changes are read about five seconds after they stop, and at least every 30 seconds while a copy goes on; a network share, a FUSE folder (mergerfs, rclone) or one past the system's limit is looked at every 30 seconds instead. A drive mounted inside a music folder after the server starts (a slow USB disk at boot) is read as it appears; one not mounted keeps its tracks and covers until it is back. A full scan runs every 6 hours (SCAN_INTERVAL_HOURS); ☰ → Rescan library runs one now, then brings Qobuz and Tidal up to date, in that order, where you are signed in with the import on.
features.folders.info: How to set up and use Music folders
features.folders.title: Music folders
features.folders.what: Any folders the server can see, added and removed in the app. Changes show by themselves: an album as it is copied in, a network share's within half a minute.
features.genres.how: Nothing to set up: they come from your files' genre tags. A genre written two ways (Indie Rock, indie rock) is one, spelled as most of your albums spell it; a Qobuz album's French genre (Électronique) shows in English (Electronic). Your files are not changed.
features.genres.info: How to set up and use Genres on pages
features.genres.title: Genres on pages
features.genres.what: An album's genres as small chips under its cover, and an artist's, the most used across their albums, in English everywhere. A tap opens that genre's albums.
features.home.how: Open ☰ → Home. Tap a row's title for all of it. To reorder rows or hide one, open Settings → Setup → Home Screen, hold a row's grip and drag it, or switch it off.
features.home.info: How to set up and use Home
features.home.title: Home
features.home.what: Rows of albums under a greeting: Not played in 6 months, Listen later, Favourites, Recently played, Smart Picks, Label of the week, Random albums, Library and Browse by genre.
features.how: How to set it up and use it.
features.labels.how: Switch it on in Settings → Setup → Record labels. Logos need a Discogs token or FanArt.tv key (Settings → Setup → API Keys). On ☰ → Labels, search and #–Z are in the top bar (on a phone or tablet, #–Z at the top right and Search in the row); hold a tile to select labels to merge.
features.labels.info: How to set up and use Record labels
features.labels.title: Record labels
features.labels.what: Labels from your files' tags or a folder level: a Labels screen, logos from Discogs and FanArt.tv, lookups for albums without a label, and merging of duplicate names.
features.later.how: On an album, ⋯ → Listen later, or select several on a wall. Open the list from ☰ → Listen later.
features.later.info: How to set up and use Listen later
features.later.title: Listen later
features.later.what: Albums put aside to play another time, on a Home row and a screen of their own. Each comes off by itself once every track has been played.
features.lead: Tap i on any feature for how to switch it on and use it. New marks what's new in v1.3.1 (v1.3.2 adds no new features).
features.levelling.how: Open Settings → Audio Devices, tap the device, and set Volume levelling (above DSP). Auto plays albums at album level and mixed tracks at track level.
features.levelling.info: How to set up and use Volume Levelling
features.levelling.title: Volume Levelling
features.levelling.what: ReplayGain per device: Off, Track, Album or Auto, a target from −14 to −25 LUFS, and a level for tracks with no loudness information.
features.library.how: Tap the Library row's title on Home, or Library in a phone's or tablet's row. Sort and Focus are in the top bar (at the top right on a phone or tablet); Focus also has Added in the last and Listening (never played, not in 6 or 12 months). ☰ → Random albums opens a shuffled wall.
features.library.info: How to set up and use Library
features.library.title: Library
features.library.what: Every album, sorted by name, artist, release date, date added, plays, last played or random, and narrowed by genre, decade, label, format, sample rate, bit depth or first letter.
features.localout.how: Install Mandarin Bridge for Linux beside the server: it plays the DAC as a room of its own. Details under Sound devices on the server.
features.localout.info: How to set up and use Sound devices on the server
features.localout.title: Sound devices on the server
features.localout.what: A USB DAC plugged into the server, played like a Sonos room by Mandarin Bridge for Linux beside it.
features.logging.how: Nothing to switch on. In a browser, Settings → Setup → Logs → Download all logs: every log as one text file, in time order. In the Android app, Settings → Setup → Logging → Save log (to Downloads/Mandarin, the server's and the Mandarin Bridges' logs with it); Clear log empties it. On Mandarin OS, the system page's Support → Download all logs. Look through it before you send it. Details under Logs.
features.logging.info: How to set up and use Logging
features.logging.title: Logging
features.logging.what: Always on: the server, every Mandarin Bridge, the Android app and the page log what happened, without personal data, kept on the server for you to send to the developer.
features.lotw.how: Switch on Settings → Setup → Record labels; the row then shows on Home.
features.lotw.info: How to set up and use Label of the week
features.lotw.title: Label of the week
features.lotw.what: With Record labels on, one label from your library on Home all week, with its albums. A new one each Monday.
features.mandarin-os.how: Write its image to a USB stick, start the PC from it and install; details under Mandarin OS. Mandarin is then at http://<box address>:3500 and the system page at http://<box address>/: storage and USB drives, the network, Mandarin Bridge, the logs, restart and shut down. It updates itself in place, and goes back by itself to the version that worked if a new one doesn't start.
features.mandarin-os.info: How to set up and use Mandarin OS
features.mandarin-os.title: Mandarin OS
features.mandarin-os.what: The recommended way to run Mandarin: a lightweight operating system made only for it, on a PC of its own, with its own system page to watch over everything.
features.mbpack.how: Open Settings → Library Scanner → MusicBrainz pack and tap Download. Folder chooses where it's kept: any folder the server can write to.
features.mbpack.info: How to set up and use MusicBrainz pack
features.mbpack.title: MusicBrainz pack
features.mbpack.what: An optional download of every MusicBrainz release with a barcode, about 2 GB on disk. Albums with a barcode are matched from it, also while musicbrainz.org is down.
features.more.how: Open any album. For the Last.fm rows, get a free key at last.fm/api/account/create and paste it in Settings → Setup → API Keys (or set LASTFM_KEY). Only albums you have are shown, each opening here; to scrobble too, see Last.fm scrobbling.
features.more.info: How to set up and use More by, and similar
features.more.title: More by, and similar
features.more.what: Under an album's review: the artist's other albums, the albums they appear on, and, with a Last.fm key, similar artists and similar albums from your own library.
features.move.how: Tap the speaker button (on the bar or Now playing) and choose the device to move to.
features.move.info: How to set up and use Move to another device
features.move.title: Move to another device
features.move.what: Pick another room, renderer or phone while music plays and it moves there: the queue goes with it, from the same track and second.
features.nowplaying.how: Tap the bar at the bottom of the screen. The waveform is off until you switch on Settings → Audio Devices → Waveform. On a large screen, Now playing can shrink to a card you drag around. On the Queue tab, hold a track to select it and more; ⋯ plays the selection now or next, or removes it; Clear all empties the queue.
features.nowplaying.info: How to set up and use Now playing
features.nowplaying.title: Now playing
features.nowplaying.what: Cover, track, transport, volume, the queue and history, and a badge saying what the device is being sent. An optional waveform seek bar is drawn from the audio.
features.offline.how: In the Android app, ☰ → Offline mode. While offline, a small Offline pill sits at the top of the screen: tap it to see why (Offline mode, or the server can't be reached).
features.offline.info: How to set up and use Offline mode
features.offline.title: Offline mode
features.offline.what: One switch: only the music on the phone shows, and the server isn't used. With no connection the app does the same by itself, and reconnects when it can.
features.onphone.how: In the app, Settings → Music Folders → On this phone and choose the folder. Selected with other albums and played on This phone, they go into the one queue.
features.onphone.info: How to set up and use Music on this phone
features.onphone.title: Music on this phone
features.onphone.what: A folder of music already on the phone, watched for changes, on Home with Focus and Sort and on artists' pages, played like the library. The server never sees it.
features.output.how: Open Settings → Audio Devices, tap a streamer or DAC, and choose a recipe under Sound, or open Advanced for each row: Mode, a filter for CD-rate and one for hi-res sources, Phase, Highest rate, Bit depth, the DAC's real bits and Dither, DSD as PCM, PCM as DSD and its Modulator, Headroom when upsampling (Auto), Gapless. All made as each track plays; an Output the server can't make in time, or the device can't play, is put back to the last that played well, and the device's page says so. Details under Upsampling and output.
features.output.info: How to set up and use Upsampling and output
features.output.title: Upsampling and output
features.output.what: For each streamer or DAC: Bit-perfect or upsampled recipes, filters in either phase, shaped dither, PCM made DSD, Headroom against clipping, and a safety net when the server falls behind.
features.phone.how: In the Android app, pick This phone with the speaker button.
features.phone.info: How to set up and use This phone
features.phone.title: This phone
features.phone.what: The phone is a player of its own: speaker, headphones or Bluetooth, with queue, history and radio. At home, your other devices can play to it while the app runs.
features.picks.how: ☰ → Smart Picks, or its Home row. Settings → Setup → Smart Picks switches it on or off and sets the hour each day's picks are made.
features.picks.info: How to set up and use Smart Picks
features.picks.title: Smart Picks
features.picks.what: Five albums a day from your own library, by artists Deezer lists as related to the ones you've played, topped up from your least-played albums.
features.pitchfork.info: How to set up and use Pitchfork
features.pitchfork.title: Pitchfork
features.pitchfork.what: Pitchfork's latest album reviews and Best New Music, read in the app, with Play on any album you own.
features.playfirst.how: Nothing to set up on Linux. Settings → Library Scanner → Processor shows the split. PLAYBACK_CORES sets how many cores playback keeps; 0 shares them all.
features.playfirst.info: How to set up and use Playback first
features.playfirst.title: Playback first
features.playfirst.what: Playback keeps a processor core of its own, two while DSP is in use. Scanning, ReplayGain and downloads run on the other cores, at the lowest priority.
features.power.how: Open the side menu (☰) and tap the power button in its top-right corner, then Restart or Shut down. On Mandarin OS the computer shuts down too; its power button starts it all again.
features.power.info: How to set up and use Restart and shut down
features.power.title: Restart and shut down
features.power.what: Restart Mandarin, or shut it down so it stops finding and controlling your speakers until you start it again.
features.qobuz.how: Settings → Services → Qobuz: sign in. Then ☰ → Qobuz to search and play; + on a cover adds an album to your Qobuz favourites (a ✓ once added) and so to the library, as does ⋯ → Add to Qobuz favourites on its page. Details under Qobuz.
features.qobuz.info: How to set up and use Qobuz
features.qobuz.title: Qobuz
features.qobuz.what: Sign in with your Qobuz subscription: your favourites and purchases become albums here, and the Qobuz browser plays anything in the catalogue, streamed through the server.
features.radio.how: Open Settings → Audio Devices, tap the device and switch on Random album radio. ⋯ → Radio on an album plays it and switches radio on for that device.
features.radio.info: How to set up and use Random Album Radio
features.radio.title: Random Album Radio
features.radio.what: When a device's queue is running out, a random album goes on the end: never one the radio played in the last six months. Switched on per device.
features.random-album.how: Choose where to play with the speaker button, then tap Random Album. Its disc turns while an album is chosen; then tap Play now, Play next or Queue, or close it.
features.random-album.info: How to set up and use Random Album
features.random-album.title: Random Album
features.random-album.what: The first tile under the greeting chooses an album you haven't played in 12 months (until Mandarin has 12 months of history, any album) and offers it to play.
features.scanner.how: Open Settings → Library Scanner. Clean up there removes albums whose files are gone, after showing counts. Matches of 85% or better are applied (with Undo); the rest are left for you to match; a copy that is every track of a bigger pressing is taken as that record. Your files are not changed. Ask iTunes too and Measure ReplayGain are on the same page; Scheduling sets the hours both run, identification first, then ReplayGain album by album.
features.scanner.info: How to set up and use Library Scanner
features.scanner.title: Library Scanner
features.scanner.what: Names albums from their files' identifiers first, then from MusicBrainz by tracks and lengths, with Apple's iTunes catalogue as a second source. Measures ReplayGain for files without it.
features.scrobble.how: Get a free key at last.fm/api/account/create and save it with its shared secret in Settings → Setup → API Keys, then tap Connect to Last.fm and allow Mandarin on Last.fm's page. A track is scrobbled at Last.fm's own point (half way or four minutes in); plays made offline or while Last.fm is down are sent when it is back. Disconnect stops it.
features.scrobble.info: How to set up and use Last.fm scrobbling
features.scrobble.title: Last.fm scrobbling
features.scrobble.what: Everything played, in every room, on a Mandarin Bridge or the phone, is scrobbled to your Last.fm account and shown there as now playing.
features.search.how: Tap the magnifying glass in the top bar (in the row at the foot of a phone's or tablet's screen) and type. Labels show when Record labels is on. Signed in to Qobuz or Tidal (Settings → Services), the service's artists and albums follow the library's, from the Library wall's filter too; tap a cover for the album's page, an artist for their page.
features.search.info: How to set up and use Search
features.search.title: Search
features.search.what: Albums, artists and labels as you type, and Qobuz's and Tidal's catalogues beside them: an album from either opens and plays whether or not it is in your library.
features.sharecard.how: Tap the share button on an album's page or Now playing; there is nothing to set up. In the Android app, Copy image puts the card on the clipboard, to paste into a forum or a message, and Download saves it to Pictures/Mandarin; in a browser, Share… or Download.
features.sharecard.info: How to set up and use Share card
features.sharecard.title: Share card
features.sharecard.what: The album as a picture: its cover, release, title and artist, its review with whose words they are, Pitchfork's score where there is one, and the duck in its corner.
features.shelf.how: Its switch is Settings → Setup → Shelf (off on a new install); off, it is off entirely and not offered. Open ☰ → Shelf, Shelf in a phone's or tablet's row, http://<server-ip>:3500/shelf, or Shelf › on the wall display; the Android app draws it itself. Swipe for one album, swipe and hold to keep turning, flick to spin; tap a spine to bring it to the front, and the one in front to open the album: the library's own album page, in the Shelf's room, with its track times, the heart, Play now, Queue and ⋯; hold a track to choose tracks and play or queue those. The choices' eight tabs (Genres, Artists, Years, Labels, Types, Formats, Favourites, Order) narrow the shelf; #N, A → Z and Z → A put the genres in order. Order has A → Z by artist, by label and catalogue number, by catalogue number, by year, and random; each device keeps the one chosen. The bar at its foot has what's playing, Spin, the zone and the volume; the queue comes in from the right.
features.shelf.info: How to set up and use Shelf
features.shelf.title: Shelf
features.shelf.what: A record shop's shelf: your albums' spines in a 3D row, narrowed by genre, artist, year, label, type, format or favourites, put in order, or spun to land anywhere.
features.signalpath.how: Play to a room and look under the album on Now playing; tap it for every step: Source, Bit depth conversion, Volume levelling where it is on, Headroom, Output with how fast it is made (Keeping up at 4.2× real time), and the device's own word; the line turns red where samples were clipped. The ✓ shows only when the device itself says the samples reach the DAC untouched. Details under Signal path.
features.signalpath.info: How to set up and use Signal path
features.signalpath.title: Signal path
features.signalpath.what: Under the album on Now playing, one short line of what goes out (Gaussian steep ×16 · 7th-order · DSD256). A tap shows each step to the DAC.
features.slim.how: Start Squeezelite on the network: it finds Mandarin by itself on port 3483, or point it at it (squeezelite -s <server-ip>). It shows in Settings → Audio Devices under its own name; switch it on. To pause at a change of rate, start it with a rate list and a delay (-r 44100-768000:500).
features.slim.info: How to set up and use Squeezelite players
features.slim.title: Squeezelite players
features.slim.what: Squeezelite players and Squeezebox-compatible hardware play from Mandarin over SlimProto, one track on into the next from their own buffer, with Output's upsampling and seeking.
features.sonos.how: Sonos rooms are found on the network by themselves (SONOS_HOSTS if not). Pick one with the speaker button; Group zones… in the same list groups them.
features.sonos.info: How to set up and use Sonos
features.sonos.title: Sonos
features.sonos.what: Play, queue, play next, shuffle, repeat and volume for each Sonos room, and grouping and ungrouping rooms. Sonos plays up to 24-bit / 48 kHz; Mandarin converts anything above.
features.sqtool.how: Open Settings → SQ-tool, choose a song and a zone (a Mandarin Bridge on Android), and press Record. Details under SQ-tool.
features.sqtool.info: How to set up and use SQ-tool
features.sqtool.title: SQ-tool
features.sqtool.what: Proves a zone's DAC gets exactly what is in the file, sample by sample: Mandarin plays a song, records what the DAC is fed, and SQ-tool compares them.
features.tags.how: Nothing to set up: tags are read with every scan.
features.tags.info: How to set up and use Every tag kept
features.tags.title: Every tag kept
features.tags.what: All of each file's tags are read into the server's database, including MusicBrainz IDs, barcode, catalogue number, ISRC and ReplayGain, and used to identify albums.
features.tidal.how: Settings → Services → Tidal → Sign in on tidal.com: open the link, sign in there, come back. Then ☰ → Tidal to search and play; + on a cover adds an album to your Tidal favourites (a ✓ once added) and so to the library, as does ⋯ → Add to Tidal favourites on its page. Details under Tidal.
features.tidal.info: How to set up and use Tidal
features.tidal.title: Tidal
features.tidal.what: Sign in with your Tidal subscription on tidal.com: your favourite albums become albums here, and the Tidal browser plays anything in the catalogue, streamed through the server.
features.touch.how: Nothing to set up: a phone or tablet gets it in the browser, the iPhone home-screen app and the Android app; a computer with a mouse keeps the top bar. Shelf is in the bar while it is switched on (Settings → Setup → Shelf). ☰, the bar's first button, opens the side menu from any screen. Tap Home or Library again to go back to the top; Search opens its field across the screen. A phone's mini player floats over the bar; a tablet's is docked on it, edge to edge. In the Android app a phone is held upright; a tablet, and a foldable opened, turns and is laid out as a tablet.
features.touch.info: How to set up and use Phones and tablets
features.touch.title: Phones and tablets
features.touch.what: On a touchscreen: a bar at the foot on every screen, Now playing too (Menu, Home, Library, Artists, Shelf, Search), and the mini player docked on it on a tablet.
features.ui.how: Open Settings → Setup → UI Settings and pick from each list; it applies at once.
features.ui.info: How to set up and use UI Settings
features.ui.title: UI Settings
features.ui.what: Text sizes, grid layout (Auto, 3 or 2 columns, or List) and tile size, saved on each device. On a desktop, text goes up to +100%.
features.unplayed.how: A Home row; tap its title for all of them. Move or hide it in Settings → Setup → Home Screen.
features.unplayed.info: How to set up and use Not played in 6 months
features.unplayed.title: Not played in 6 months
features.unplayed.what: Albums you haven't played in six months. The row stays hidden until Mandarin has six months of your listening.
features.untagged.how: Nothing to set up. Those albums are then looked up by the Library Scanner like any other.
features.untagged.info: How to set up and use Untagged files named from folders
features.untagged.title: Untagged files named from folders
features.untagged.what: A file with no tags takes its artist, album, year, title and track number from its folder and file names. Nothing is written to your files.
features.updates.how: Settings → Updates → Check for update beside the server, the Android app (in the app) or a Bridge; once it says Update available, tap it again. The server starts again in a few seconds, the app's update goes to Android's installer, a Linux or Raspberry Pi Bridge updates itself, and an Android Bridge shows a notification whose tap downloads the update in its browser. The server and the Bridges install only an update signed with Mandarin's release key.
features.updates.info: How to set up and use Updates
features.updates.title: Updates
features.updates.what: The server updates itself from GitHub and checks every 12 hours. The Android app and every Mandarin Bridge have their own Check for update beside the server's.
features.upnp.how: A renderer found on the network is off until you switch it on in Settings → Audio Devices. Then pick it with the speaker button. Look again searches the network now. Where MPD is found beside it (a Chord Poly), Output → Player → Its own player hands MPD the queue, and Output → Gapless → Albums as one stream sends an album as one stream however the device joins files.
features.upnp.info: How to set up and use UPnP/DLNA renderers
features.upnp.title: UPnP/DLNA renderers
features.upnp.what: WiiM, Chord Poly, streamers, AV receivers and TVs on your network, played like a Sonos room, gapless; one with MPD beside it can be handed the whole queue.
features.usbdac.how: Plug the DAC in. It shows on This phone's page in Settings → Audio Devices; switch on USB direct there. Pull it out while playing and the phone pauses, as when headphones come out.
features.usbdac.info: How to set up and use USB DAC on the phone
features.usbdac.title: USB DAC on the phone
features.usbdac.what: The app's own USB Audio driver plays to a DAC on the phone's port at the file's rate and depth, without Android's mixer; DSD natively or as DoP.
features.wall.how: Open http://<server-ip>:3500/display on the screen. Its switch (on by default) and options are in Settings → Setup → Wall Display; off, it is off entirely. Tap the screen for its controls; Shelf › opens Shelf.
features.wall.info: How to set up and use Wall display
features.wall.title: Wall display
features.wall.what: A full-screen now playing page for a TV or tablet; on a big TV its reviews and covers are drawn large enough to read from across the room.
formats.doc-title: What each device is sent · Mandarin
formats.lead: Each track goes the way the device can take it, and the Now playing badge says what was sent.
formats.top.h32: Its own ceiling, read from the device
formats.top.h37: Formats nothing plays as they are
formats.top.p1: Within that, the file as stored. Above it, or in a format Sonos can't read, FLAC at 24/48.
formats.top.p2: Within it, the file as stored. Above it, FLAC at the highest rate the device takes in the file's family. Upsampled ×2, ×4 or Max if you choose (Upsampling and output). DSD goes as the DSF or DFF file itself to a device that says it takes DSD files, as PCM otherwise.
formats.top.p3: Every rate, depth and DSD rate the DAC says it takes, read from the Bridge itself: the file as it is within them, DSD natively or as DoP. Mandarin Bridge.
formats.top.p4: Over SlimProto, a continuous stream of PCM; DSD as the DSF or DFF itself, natively or as DoP.
formats.top.p5: FLAC, or upsampled; DSD as DSF where it takes it. One track plays on into the next from its own buffer.
formats.top.p6: The file as stored within 24/48, FLAC 24/48 above it. Away from home, Opus 256 by default.
formats.top.p7: The file at its own rate and depth where the DAC takes it, DSD natively or as DoP, FLAC at the DAC's highest rate otherwise.
formats.top.p8: APE, WavPack, WMA Lossless, 24-bit WAV, more than two channels: FLAC, in stereo.
formats.top.p9: Conversion is ffmpeg with the SoX resampler and triangular dither. A converted track is written to a cache as it plays, so the device starts on the first frames, and the next tracks in the queue are prepared ahead. Replays come from the cache (4 GB by default, least recently played removed first).
how-it-works.development.li1: The end-to-end test starts two fake Sonos rooms on 127.0.0.11/12:1400, plays a CD-quality album and a 24/96 album through the real server, and checks what the "speaker" fetched: bit-perfect FLAC for the first, FLAC 24/48 for the second. It needs ffmpeg on the PATH (or FFMPEG_PATH).
how-it-works.development.li2: The browser tests open the page itself in headless Chromium or Chrome — at a desktop with a mouse, a phone and a tablet — and check Home, the album view and Now playing. They use the browser already installed (or CHROME_PATH), with no extra packages, and are skipped where there is none.

how-it-works.development.li4: The site's languages: npm run i18n writes every marked text of these pages into docs/i18n/en.json, the translators' source; the tests fail while a language file's keys or its links, code and markup differ from it.

how-it-works.lead: Mandarin is a server and an Android app. The server scans your library and plays it to Sonos rooms, UPnP/DLNA streamers, Mandarin Bridges and the Android app.
how-it-works.playback-first.p1: On Linux with three cores or more, playback (what Mandarin makes as a track plays: its conversion, upsampling or DSD) keeps a core of its own, or two while DSP is in use (the last ones), and the server runs on the others. Scanning, measuring ReplayGain, the tag reader check and the phone's downloads run at the lowest priority, their disk reads last; conversions made ahead of play run just below playback. Settings → Library Scanner → Processor shows the split. PLAYBACK_CORES=1 or 2 fixes how many cores playback keeps, 0 shares every core; PLAYBACK_CORE=<n> picks the core.
how-it-works.playback-first.title: Playback comes first
how-it-works.sound-devices.p1: On Linux, Mandarin plays no sound device of its own (v1.2.1). A USB DAC on the computer Mandarin runs on is played by Mandarin Bridge for Linux, installed beside it with one line, and the DAC is a room of its own in Settings → Audio Devices. On Mandarin OS, choose Mandarin Bridge as it installs, or Install it from the system page's Settings tab. The server used to open the computer's sound cards itself (ALSA), kept losing the DAC and competed with the Bridge for it. A card it had in Audio Devices is forgotten by itself.
how-it-works.sound-devices.title: Sound devices on the server
how-it-works.top.li1: Library. The music folders are walked and every audio file's tags are read into a database (SQLite). Albums are decided a folder at a time, so a folder of tracks by different artists with no album-artist tag becomes one compilation, and CD1/CD2 folders become one album. Covers come from cover.jpg/folder.jpg/… or the first track's embedded picture, resized once per size and cached; an album with no cover gets one drawn, with its title. The pictures are drawn with ffmpeg. Rescans only re-read files whose size or date changed, on the cores playback doesn't keep.
how-it-works.top.li2: Album names. The identification scan looks each album up by what its files carry (a release id, barcode, catalogue number, ISRCs), then by name on MusicBrainz and iTunes. It scores each release against the tracks and their lengths, and lays the names over the album, never on the files, with the MusicBrainz pack, loudness measuring and the waveforms alongside. Every MusicBrainz request waits its turn on one timer, and while MusicBrainz is turning requests away every lookup pauses (a minute, then twice as long each time, an hour at most).
how-it-works.top.li3: Credits and artists. In the background, one album and one act at a time at MusicBrainz's pace, the server reads who played, sang, wrote and made each album from its tags and its MusicBrainz release, and who each act is (members, years, place, links) from MusicBrainz and Wikidata, with a picture from FanArt.tv, Wikidata or Deezer. A page asked for before it gets there is looked up there and then, as the act its albums are by: the MusicBrainz id in their tags or matches, else the act MusicBrainz lists for their titles. Names found to share a MusicBrainz id are one artist, written as MusicBrainz names them; two acts of one name with their own ids are two. Kept in the database; your files are not changed.
how-it-works.top.li4: Streamers. Found on the network by SSDP, each one's description read for what it can play (plus a WiiM's own API), every device kept in a register with your names and settings, and played through its own transport (AVTransport): the queue kept on the server, the next track handed over ahead of time (gapless where it supports it), changes arriving by UPnP events. The stream plans decide what each device gets: the file itself within its ceiling, FLAC at its highest rate or upsampled in 64-bit float otherwise.
how-it-works.top.li5: Sonos. One speaker is found over SSDP and the whole household is read from it (ZoneGroupTopology). A Sonos group is a zone (its coordinator owns the queue) and each room is an output (volume and mute are per room). Tracks go into the coordinator's own Sonos queue, with the DIDL-Lite metadata Sonos insists on, so the speaker moves between tracks by itself. The queue you see is read back from the speaker, so anything added from the Sonos app appears too. Ported from Caldera Sonos Bridge and the UPnP to Sonos bridge, by the same author.
how-it-works.top.li6: Audio. Each queued item is an address on the server. Within 24/48 it serves the file as stored, with byte ranges; above that, ffmpeg writes FLAC 24/48 to the cache and the speaker is served from the growing file.
how-it-works.top.li7: The interface. Mandarin's own page, served by the server and shown in the browser and the iPhone home-screen app, talking to the server's /api. The Android app draws the same screens natively and asks the same /api.
how-it-works.top.li8: The server. One program in C# (.NET, built to a single self-contained file: no .NET or Node.js needed to run it). It began in v0.8.1 as a front door before the original Node.js server, took its parts over one by one with each held to the Node server's own answers, and has been the whole server since v0.9.0.
how-it-works.top.p1: Tracks go into the speaker's own Sonos queue; a streamer is handed each next track ahead of time. Each device fetches the audio from the server: the file itself when it can play it, converted to what it takes when it can't.
how-it-works.top.p2: For how your music is found and named, in plain words, there is a guide on Downloads.

install.top.li2: On Linux, the alternative: natively on a Debian, Ubuntu or Raspberry Pi OS machine you already run, beside what else it does, with one command.
install.updating.li1: Linux and the Raspberry Pi: in a few seconds, by itself. The new build goes in the Bridge's data folder and the program installed hands over to it as it starts again; one that fails as it starts is let go, and the installed one runs on.
install.updating.li2: Android: Update puts a notification on the device; its tap downloads the update in the browser, and Android's installer asks you to install it. The Bridge holds no permission to install apps itself.
install.updating.li3: An Android Bridge from before v0.2.1, or a Linux or Raspberry Pi Bridge from before v0.3.1, needs one last update by hand, from Downloads.
install.updating.li4: A numbered Mandarin follows the Bridges' numbered releases (Mandarin Bridge v0.3.10 with Mandarin v1.3.2).
install.updating.p1: In the app: Settings → Updates → Check for update beside the server → Update available. The server downloads the new release from GitHub, checks it against the release's sums, swaps it in and starts again in a few seconds; a browser's page reloads on its own. In the Android app the app has its own Check for update beside it, and each Mandarin Bridge has a row of its own. It also checks twice a day and shows a banner when a new version is out. On Mandarin OS, Mandarin updates the same way, and Mandarin OS itself from its system page (Updating Mandarin OS).
install.updating.p2: Mandarin's server is one program, in C#. An update from the app fetches that program of the new version for your machine (x64 or ARM64) from the release, checks it against the release's sums and its signature with Mandarin's release key (a release replaced along with its sums is refused), puts it and the new page in place, and starts again in the same process — a few seconds. If it can't start again in place, it stops and its systemd service starts it again.
install.updating.p3: The new program is checked and laid in beside the old before anything is swapped: if something fails after the swap, the old one (kept as mandarin-server.prev) is put back, and a folder the release can't be written over is named before anything is changed.
install.updating.p4: Every Bridge Mandarin knows, on Android, Linux or a Raspberry Pi, has a row of its own on Settings → Updates, its name and version, and its own Check for update, as the server's and the app's rows: it asks GitHub now and becomes Update available when a newer build is published for it (the rows also find one by themselves within a minute or so). A tap on Update available asks the Bridge to update itself: it fetches the release from GitHub, checks it against the checksum published with it and its signature with Mandarin's release key, and puts it in place.

logs.kept.p1: The server keeps every log in its data folder's Logs: its own in MandarinServer_log.txt, then .01 to .20 older (8 MB each), every Bridge's in Bridges, every app's in Apps (by the phone's name) and the page's in Web, each rolled so none grows without end. A Bridge keeps its own log too, in files in its data folder. The app keeps its own in its storage (two files of 3 MB at most) and sends its new lines to the server every five minutes and as the log is saved. On Mandarin OS the shared folder has them, read-only: MandarinServer's Logs, MandarinBridge, MandarinApp and MandarinOS.
logs.kept.title: Where it is kept
logs.lead: Mandarin keeps a log always, everywhere it runs: the server, every Mandarin Bridge, the Android app and the page in a browser. There is nothing to switch on, and it can't be switched off, so a fault seen once is already in the log.
logs.send.fine1: It keeps what helps find a fault: home-network addresses, the names of rooms and devices, what was playing, error messages.
logs.send.li1: In a browser: Settings → Setup → Logs → Download all logs gives one text file: every log Mandarin keeps (the server's, every Bridge's, every app's and the page's) merged in time order, each line saying where it came from, and at its head what this server is (its version, how it is installed, the system) and each log's own header. The same page shows the server's newest lines, narrowed by level and by what they hold.
logs.send.li10: The Mandarin Bridges: every Bridge Mandarin knows, under its name: what it logs (the player, the DAC, a recording, an update), gathered by the server every five minutes.
logs.send.li11: The page: what goes wrong in a browser's page (an error nothing caught), under the browser's name.
logs.send.li12: The server: each line it logs, with what is yours alone taken out: what it is as each file begins, how it is every five minutes (memory, threads, free space), and an error with its stack.
logs.send.li16: Your own home folder's name in a path.
logs.send.li2: In the Android app: Settings → Setup → Logging says how much the app has logged and since when. Save log saves the app's log, the server's and each Mandarin Bridge's together, as one text file, to Downloads/Mandarin on the phone; Clear log empties the app's log and the server's own, and logging goes on.
logs.send.li3: On Mandarin OS: the system page's Support → Download all logs gives every log on the box as one text file in time order, Mandarin OS's own and the system's with Mandarin's, and the shared folder holds them, read-only (Mandarin OS).
logs.send.li4: Screens: each screen opened and how long after the tap, what is on screen, where each tap fell, and anything that doesn't flow: a screen shown for a moment between two others, one opened and closed by itself, a frame that stalls.
logs.send.li5: Requests: each request the app makes to the server: its address on the server, how long it took and whether it worked. The values in it are left out.
logs.send.li6: The way to the server: home, away (Tailscale) or offline, and networks coming and going.
logs.send.li7: The phone's player: playing or paused, the track's number in the queue, its position and the volume.
logs.send.li8: The app: its memory, crashes and freezes, and Android's own lines for Mandarin.
logs.send.li9: The app's Tailscale: whether it is running and the CPU time it has used, and when it is stopped, why, with its last lines (addresses taken out).
logs.send.p1: The logs are made without personal data, and you are told so where you save them. Please look through a log before you send it: what you send is your choice.
logs.send.title: To send the logs to the developer
logs.top.p1: Each line is dated in UTC with its level (INFO, WARN, ERROR), so every device's lines sort together. Nothing in them is sent anywhere unless you send it.
