mandarin-os.using.li10: networkreset: the network back to DHCP, and the computer started again. For a static address that lost the box.
mandarin-os.using.li11: passwordreset: Mandarin's account removed and every device signed out, for a forgotten password. Your library, edits and history stay; create the account again in a browser.
mandarin-os.using.li12: On the system page: Settings shows Mandarin OS's version and, when a newer one is out, Update and restart (with the shared folder's password). It downloads the new version into the data partition, checks its checksum and its signature (Mandarin's release key, as Mandarin's own updates), writes it beside this one, and starts the computer again on it: music stops for a few minutes. Check for updates looks at once.
mandarin-os.using.li13: By itself: the weekly upkeep puts a newer version in, while nothing plays, and starts the computer again only when nothing plays.
mandarin-os.using.li14: If it doesn't start, or starts without what the box needs (the data partition, the shared folder, the network, the system page, and Mandarin if it answered before), the computer tries it three times, then goes back by itself to the version that worked, which the update never touched. The system page then says the update didn't start and the box went back to the version before. The weekly upkeep never tries that version again; Update and restart can.
mandarin-os.using.li15: What is kept: everything on the data partition (your music, Mandarin's library and settings) and on USB drives is never touched. The box's own settings are carried into the new version: the shared folder's user, password and its files' owner, the network as set (a static address included), Mandarin Bridge if installed, and Mandarin itself where the one running is newer than the image's (it is never put back to an older one).
mandarin-os.using.li2: Storage: the data partition's space; each USB drive, whether it is read-only and why, and Eject before you unplug it; a Linux drive from another computer made the shared folder's; internal storage, where another internal disk can be formatted for it (you type erase first; never the system's disk or a USB drive).
mandarin-os.using.li3: Network & Access: the address now; DHCP or a static address, which is checked before it is taken and put back by itself after two minutes unless you keep it from the new address; a connection test, layer by layer; the shared folder and its user.
mandarin-os.using.li4: Settings: Mandarin OS's version, with Update and restart when a newer one is out and Check for updates (below); Mandarin Bridge installed or removed (for a USB DAC plugged into the box), and the weekly upkeep's last run.
mandarin-os.using.li5: Support: every log on the box as one text file (Download all logs), and Mandarin's, Mandarin OS's and the system's logs read and filtered on the page; Reinstall Mandarin (put back from its latest release, your library, settings and music kept) and Reset Mandarin (it starts as new, its library, account and settings set aside in its Backups folder, not deleted).
mandarin-os.using.li6: The power menu (⏻, top right): restart Mandarin, restart the computer, or shut it down.
mandarin-os.using.li7: Storage: copy your music in here. Each USB drive plugged in is under Storage/USB, by its name, and internal storage is Storage/Internal.
mandarin-os.using.li9: MandarinServer, MandarinBridge, MandarinApp and MandarinOS: the logs (and Mandarin's backups), read-only.
mandarin-os.using.note1: The box's address. Everything below is reached at the box's address on your network, such as 192.168.0.57: its screen shows it, and so does your router's list of devices. Reserve that address for the box in your router (a DHCP reservation, or a static address on the system page's Network & Access tab) so it never changes. Computers and iPhones usually find the box as mandarin.local too, and mandarin works where the router names the devices on its network; an Android phone often finds neither. The address always works.
mandarin-os.using.note2: Installed with 0.1.3 or earlier? Those can't update themselves (the updater came with 0.1.4, and the users their files belong to are numbered otherwise): reinstall 0.1.6 once from the USB stick. Reinstalling erases the system disk, the data partition with it (Mandarin's library and settings, and music copied into Storage on that disk), so first make a backup in Mandarin (Settings → Backup & restore, Back up to the server) and copy it off the box from the shared folder (MandarinServer/Backups), with any music in Storage; afterwards, restore it in Mandarin from that file. Music on USB drives isn't on the system disk and isn't touched. From 0.1.4 on, it updates itself.
mandarin-os.using.p1: Mandarin is at http://<box address>:3500. It is the same Mandarin as everywhere: the app, the web page, Sonos, the streamers and Bridges, Qobuz and Tidal, its settings. Its music folder is the shared folder's Storage, USB drives and internal storage included. Shut down in Mandarin (☰, the power button) shuts the computer down too; its power button starts it all again.
mandarin-os.using.p10: From 0.1.4, Mandarin OS updates itself in place, without reinstalling. The system disk has two system partitions: the version running is on one, and a new version is written onto the other, never over the one running. The box looks for a newer version once a day.
mandarin-os.using.p2: http://<box address>/ (no port) is Mandarin OS's own page. Anyone at home can read it; every change asks for the shared folder's password (five wrong in five minutes, and it stops trying for five minutes).
mandarin-os.using.p3: smb://<box address>/data, or \\<box address>\Data on Windows, with the user name and password chosen at install.
mandarin-os.using.p4: A USB drive is mounted as it is plugged in, checked first, and its music is in Mandarin: ext4, exFAT, FAT and NTFS, and a Mac drive (HFS+) read-only. One whose filesystem can't be repaired is mounted read-only, and the system page says why. Eject it on the system page before you unplug it.
mandarin-os.using.p5: A Linux drive (ext4) from another computer keeps the owners its files were given there: the shared folder copies music from it, but moving, renaming or deleting on it is refused (“Access denied”). The system page's Storage tab says so beside the drive; Make them the shared folder's (with the shared folder's password) makes its files the shared folder's, and then they can be moved, renamed and deleted. Only that drive is changed, and a big one takes a few minutes. exFAT, FAT and NTFS drives need nothing: they are the shared folder's as they are plugged in.
mandarin-os.using.p6: With a screen plugged in, the box shows its version, where to find Mandarin, the system page and the shared folder, and whether Mandarin is running. It takes two words, typed with a keyboard and then confirmed with yes:
mandarin-os.using.p7: There is no login and no SSH: the screen and the system page are the ways in.
mandarin-os.using.p8: Once a week, when nothing is playing (no room playing, no scan under way), Mandarin OS takes a newer Mandarin OS where one is out (below), or else Debian's security updates, removes what nothing needs any more, restarts only if an update needs it, and then checks that everything works, starting again whatever isn't. Each step is in its log.
mandarin-os.using.p9: Mandarin and Mandarin Bridge update from Mandarin's Settings → Updates, as everywhere (Updating).
mandarin-os.using.title: Using Mandarin OS
mandarin-os.what.li1: Lightweight: Debian 13 with Mandarin installed natively, and nothing else: no desktop, no login, no SSH. Everything coming in from the network is refused by a firewall, but what Mandarin and the system answer.
mandarin-os.what.li2: Its own web page: the system page, http://<box address>/, shows Mandarin, its services, the storage, the network and the logs, and does what you'd otherwise need a shell for: eject a drive, set a static address, install Mandarin Bridge, reinstall or reset Mandarin, restart or shut down.
mandarin-os.what.li3: A shared folder for your music: smb://<box address>/data. Copy music in from any computer, or plug in a USB drive: it is mounted, and in Mandarin, as it is plugged in.
mandarin-os.what.li4: Looks after itself: once a week, when nothing is playing, it takes a newer Mandarin OS or Debian's security updates, clears out what isn't needed, and checks that everything works.
mandarin-os.what.li5: Updates itself in place: a new version is written beside the one running, never over it, and started; if it doesn't start, the box goes back to the version that worked by itself. Your music, settings and drives aren't touched. Updating Mandarin OS
mandarin-os.what.p1: A music server should be something you switch on and forget. Mandarin OS turns a small computer into exactly that: Mandarin and only what Mandarin needs, installed from a USB stick in a few minutes, with nothing else to set up or keep up to date. That is why it is the recommended way to run Mandarin; to run Mandarin on a Linux machine you already have instead, see Install on Linux, the alternative.
mandarin-os.what.title: What it is, and why
services.lead: With a subscription of your own, Qobuz's and Tidal's albums live in Mandarin beside your files: your favourites on the walls, their catalogues in search, every track streamed through the server.
services.qobuz.li1: A subscriber signs in (Settings → Services → Qobuz). Mandarin keeps the sign-in token, never the password. Qobuz decides what the account may stream.
services.qobuz.li2: Your favourites and purchases are albums here — every one, brought up to date shortly after signing in, every six hours, and when you add a favourite: on the walls, in search, Smart Picks and Listen later, with a Qobuz mark on the cover. Favourites and purchases in the library on the Services page switches this off.
services.qobuz.li3: Favourites follow both ways, by themselves (v0.7.3). Remove an album from your Qobuz favourites here and it is gone from Qobuz and off the walls within the moment; add one and it is on them. A favourite added or removed in the Qobuz app follows here on the next look: the server checks every two minutes, and the page checks when you come back to Home or the Library wall. An album's page says why it is in the library — a favourite or a purchase since a date, or only played — and its release date when it is not out yet.
services.qobuz.li4: The Qobuz browser (☰ → Qobuz): search, new releases, best sellers, most streamed, press awards, editor's picks, an artist's albums, as the album grid the rest of Mandarin draws, each cover with its + for your Qobuz favourites. Tapping an album opens its page here, the same page as any album: Play now, Play next, Queue, or from a track, to the zone chosen. An album played without being kept is known here for a month (its page, Now playing, history) and stays off the walls.
services.qobuz.li5: Signed out, it all steps aside: Qobuz albums leave the walls while their rows stay, so signing in puts everything straight back. Clean up on the Library Scanner page removes what's no longer wanted — Qobuz albums not in your favourites or purchases (all of them while signed out), and, separately, albums whose files are gone from the server — after showing you the counts; plays stay in history.
services.qobuz.li6: Two favourites, kept apart. The + on a Qobuz album's cover in the browser (a ✓ once added), and Add to Qobuz favourites / Remove from Qobuz favourites in the ⋯ menu on the album's page here, are your Qobuz favourite, and that is what puts the album in the library. The heart is Mandarin's own favourite, as on any album.
services.qobuz.li7: Every track is streamed through the server: when a player comes to fetch it, Mandarin asks Qobuz for that one track (a signed request, as Qobuz requires) and feeds the player from its transcode cache — a Sonos room gets 24/48 at most, a streamer or a USB DAC what it takes, the phone what its DAC takes, with DSP and Volume Levelling as for a file. The next track is made ready behind the one playing, so albums play gaplessly. Stream quality on the Services page sets the most asked for (CD, Hi-Res 24/96, Hi-Res 24/192); the subscription sets the ceiling.
services.qobuz.li8: Every play is reported to Qobuz (its streaming start and end), as Qobuz's own apps report them, so artists are paid. Nothing is downloaded: a Qobuz album has no Download to this phone, no Edit album, no waveform, and is not in offline mode; the cache holds only what the queue needs, pruned as the cache fills, and plays nothing once the account is signed out.
services.qobuz.p1: Mandarin streams from Qobuz with a Qobuz subscription (v0.6.23), the way the Lyrion Music Server's Qobuz plugin does — the same API, the same credentials, the same rules. Experimental, in line with Qobuz's terms of service; those who use it do so at their own risk.
services.qobuz.p2: The app id and secret are the ones the Lyrion plugin carries, as Qobuz answers no application requests; Qobuz leaves that plugin be because of how it behaves, and Mandarin behaves the same.
services.tidal.li1: A subscriber signs in on tidal.com (Settings → Services → Tidal → Sign in on tidal.com): Mandarin shows a link and a code, you sign in there on any device, and Mandarin notices by itself. It keeps the sign-in token, renewed as Tidal requires, never a password.
services.tidal.li2: Your favourite albums are albums here, every one, with a Tidal mark on the cover; Favourites in the library on the Services page switches this off. Favourites follow both ways, by themselves (v0.7.3), as with Qobuz: removed here, gone from Tidal and the walls at once; changed in the Tidal app, here on the next look (two minutes, or when you come back to Home).
services.tidal.li3: The Tidal browser (☰ → Tidal): search, new releases, recommended, top, rising, an artist's albums, as the album grid, each cover with its + for your Tidal favourites; an album opens on its page here. The ⋯ menu on a Tidal album's page has Add to Tidal favourites / Remove from Tidal favourites.
services.tidal.li4: The stream. Stream quality on the Services page is CD (FLAC 16/44.1) or Hi-Res: Tidal's hi-res FLAC, up to 24/192, where an album has it and the subscription allows. Tidal sends hi-res as MPEG-DASH (an initialisation piece and numbered segments), which the server joins into one stream for ffmpeg on its own loopback; where Tidal answers a hi-res ask with anything else, CD quality is asked for instead. What Tidal actually streams a track at is learnt the first time it is played and the album's badge corrected. Tidal has no play reports.
services.tidal.p1: Mandarin streams from Tidal with a Tidal subscription (v0.6.24), the way the Lyrion Music Server's Tidal plugin does — the same API, the same credentials, the same rules — and Tidal albums live in Mandarin exactly as Qobuz albums do (above): the walls, the browser, Clean up, the two favourites, the server's transcode cache, nothing downloaded. Experimental, in line with Tidal's terms of service; those who use it do so at their own risk.
services.tidal.p2: The client id and secret are the ones the Lyrion plugin carries, as Tidal's developer programme answers no streaming requests; Tidal leaves that plugin be because of how it behaves, and Mandarin behaves the same.
signal-path.lead: Under the album on Now playing, one short line of what goes out, such as Gaussian steep ×16 · 7th-order · DSD256. A tap shows every step from the file to what the DAC is fed, in as few as it can be.
signal-path.proof-is-sq.p1: The signal path says only what is known, and whose word it is. Whether every sample reaches the DAC is for a recording of what it was fed to prove: that is SQ-tool.
signal-path.proof-is-sq.title: Proof is SQ-tool's job
signal-path.reading-it.figcaption1: Now playing with its signal path open: the file, the output to FiiO R7 USB, and what its DAC is fed.
signal-path.reading-it.li1: Padded to 32 bits for the DAC: the DAC takes 32-bit words, so each 16-bit sample goes in one with zeros below it; its value is unchanged. Where the device doesn't say the samples go untouched, it reads sent as 32-bit instead.
signal-path.reading-it.li2: Fixed volume: the samples untouched: the volume is the DAC's or the amplifier's, so Mandarin never scales the samples. Otherwise the step says the level they are scaled by.
signal-path.reading-it.li3: The ✓ beside the format shows only when the device itself says the samples reach the DAC untouched in the format sent. Mandarin Bridge says it; a WiiM's own API says only the format, so it has none.
signal-path.reading-it.p1: In the picture, the FiiO R7's Bridge reports “PCM 44.1 kHz, the 16-bit samples padded to 32 bits for the DAC, fixed volume: the samples untouched — as Mandarin Bridge reports it”.
signal-path.reading-it.title: Reading it
signal-path.top.span1: The track as it is stored, such as FLAC 16-bit 44.1 kHz 2ch.
signal-path.top.span2: Where Mandarin works the samples (upsampling, DSD made from PCM, the DSP): they are decoded to 64-bit float and worked there, 16-bit to 64-bit float. A stream only passed on has none.
signal-path.top.span3: Where it is on: the level and how it was found, −7.3 dB · ReplayGain.
signal-path.top.span4: Where Headroom when upsampling turns a track down so its peaks between samples don't clip (v1.2.5), by how much.
signal-path.top.span5: What goes out, in one line: the filter, the modulator and the format, such as Gaussian steep ×16 · 7th-order · DSD256 or Long ×2 · 24/88.2 kHz, with the dither where Mandarin makes it, and how fast it is made as it plays (Keeping up at 4.2× real time). Red where samples were clipped, with how many and how far over. Now playing's line under the title is this same line.
signal-path.top.span6: What the device itself reports feeding its DAC: the format, how the samples sit in the DAC's words, and whether its volume touches them — said as the device's own word.

sq-tool.lead: SQ-tool proves whether a zone's DAC gets exactly what is in the file, sample by sample. It is part of Mandarin: Settings → SQ-tool.
sq-tool.next: Next: What each device is sent →
sq-tool.test-screen-by.figcaption1: Settings → SQ-tool opens it in its own tab.
sq-tool.test-screen-by.figcaption2: Start a new test: choose a song from the music folder, then the zone to record on. Earlier tests are listed below.
sq-tool.test-screen-by.figcaption3: The result for the FiiO R7's Bridge: Helldriver, FLAC 16-bit, 44.1 kHz, 2:41, recorded whole — bit-perfect, its DAC fed exactly the samples in the file.
sq-tool.test-screen-by.figcaption4: Spectrograms of the file and of what the DAC was fed, on one colour scale, down to −180 dB. Drag across one to zoom in; tap to read the time and frequency.
sq-tool.test-screen-by.figcaption5: The same with the frequency scale Linear instead of Log.
sq-tool.test-screen-by.figcaption6: The difference: one recording subtracted from the other, sample by sample. Black means the samples are identical.
sq-tool.test-screen-by.figcaption7: Charts: the average spectrum, the level over time and the bit usage. Identical data draws identical lines, one on top of the other; the 16-bit song fills 16 bits of the 32-bit words.
sq-tool.test-screen-by.figcaption8: Details side by side: format, rate, bits in use, length, silence, peak, loudness, clipped samples, and the fingerprint — the same fingerprint means the same sample data.
sq-tool.test-screen-by.figcaption9: Downloads: the song, what the DAC was fed, and the difference, as WAV files.

sq-tool.what-it-needs.li1: Mandarin OS and the Linux installer bring what it needs (Python 3 and numpy).
sq-tool.what-it-needs.li2: Installed by hand: add Python 3 and numpy (sudo apt install python3 python3-numpy on Debian or Ubuntu); until then its page says what is missing. SQTOOL_PYTHON names another Python to run it with.
sq-tool.what-it-needs.li3: Mandarin starts SQ-tool the first time it is opened, on a port of the computer only, behind your sign-in, with its data in the data folder's sq-tool.
sq-tool.what-it-needs.li4: An update made from Settings brings it (from the first release that carries it); Python and numpy are the computer's to have.

troubleshooting.lead: http://<server-ip>:3500/api/health answers without signing in; /api/status (signed in) says what the server can see.
troubleshooting.top.h35: Asked to sign in with the sign-in off
troubleshooting.top.h38: DoP from a Linux Bridge, native DSD from Android
troubleshooting.top.h39: A click as the rate changes
troubleshooting.top.p1: Check the server is on the same network (subnet) as the speakers, then look at sonos.error in /api/status. Setting SONOS_HOSTS to one speaker's IP skips discovery.
troubleshooting.top.p10: Its own screen (a screen plugged in) shows its address. A static address that lost the box: type networkreset there, then yes, and it goes back to DHCP and starts again. Everything about it is on the system page, http://<box address>/; see Mandarin OS.
troubleshooting.top.p11: Open its page (http://<it>:49494/, or the Android app itself) to see that it runs and which DAC it plays to, then Look again in Settings → Audio Devices. A Bridge found is off until you switch it on there.
troubleshooting.top.p2: The speakers can't reach the server. On a machine with several network interfaces set SERVER_IP to its LAN address, and check nothing blocks the port.
troubleshooting.top.p3: /api/status shows music_dir and index_count. Check the music folder is there and that the folder is readable. On Mandarin OS, copy music into the shared folder's Storage (smb://<box address>/data), or plug in a USB drive and see it on the system page's Storage tab.
troubleshooting.top.p4: /api/health must say "ffmpeg": true. Mandarin OS and the Linux installer bring it; a hand-run server needs ffmpeg on the PATH.
troubleshooting.top.p5: Without a sign-in, a device must ask by a name used at home (an address, a bare name, or one ending .local, .lan, .home.arpa or .ts.net), from your home network or tailnet. Behind a reverse proxy on the same machine, the proxy must pass on who asked. See Your account.
troubleshooting.top.p6: The app says so when Android ended it while you weren't using it, with Android's own words. If it comes back, save the log (Settings → Setup → Logging → Save log, or Download all logs in a browser) and send it (Logs).
troubleshooting.top.p7: On Mandarin OS, type passwordreset at its screen; on Linux, sudo -u mandarin env DATA_DIR=/var/lib/mandarin /opt/mandarin/server/bin/mandarin-server reset-password. Then create the account again from a device at home.
troubleshooting.top.p8: Linux's USB audio driver offers a DAC native DSD only where its own list knows the DAC's maker; any other is given DSD as DoP. The Bridge's page (http://<it>:49494/) and log say when the kernel holds it back, with the one line for /etc/modprobe.d that frees it; then unplug the DAC and plug it in again. See Mandarin Bridge.
troubleshooting.top.p9: A Mandarin Bridge gives its DAC half a second of silence at a change of rate between tracks. A Squeezelite player pauses for as long as its -r option says: start it with -r 44100-768000:500.
upsampling.dsp.p1: Below Output, a device's DSP: a parametric EQ of up to ten bands, headphone profiles from AutoEq, and room correction from an impulse response (a WAV from REW, Dirac or a headphone measurement), one for each rate or a zip of them. A device's DSP runs in this order: volume levelling, then the headroom, then the DSP at the track's own rate, then upsampling.
upsampling.for-bit-perfect.p1: Choose Bit-perfect under the device's Output (Mode Original) and set its volume to fixed (or the DAC's own): upsampling, DSD from PCM, DSP, volume levelling and a volume in software all change the samples, on purpose. The signal path shows what was done, and SQ-tool proves it.
upsampling.for-bit-perfect.title: For a bit-perfect result
upsampling.headroom-clipping-shown.p1: A track mastered to full scale has peaks between its samples above it, which upsampling would clip. Each making counts the samples it clips: Now playing's upsampling line turns red, and the signal path says how many and how far over. Headroom when upsampling, in a device's Output, is Auto by default: a track Mandarin upsamples, or makes DSD of, is turned down by what its true peak needs after levelling, and half a dB more (DSD's own room allowed for); a track that doesn't need it keeps its level. Off leaves every track as it is.
upsampling.headroom-clipping-shown.title: Headroom, and clipping shown
upsampling.keeping-up-safety.p1: A track made as it plays says in its signal path how fast it is made (Keeping up at 4.2× real time); slower than real time, Now playing says it is falling behind. Each device keeps the Output that last played well: an Output this server can't make in time, or that the device can't play, is put back to that one, the track playing on from where it was, and the device's page says what happened. Never for a Qobuz or Tidal stream.
upsampling.keeping-up-safety.title: Keeping up, and a safety net
upsampling.lead: Each streamer, DAC, Mandarin Bridge or Squeezelite player has its own Output: play the file as it is, or upsample it, make it DSD, and choose how far it goes. Settings → Audio Devices → a device → Output.
upsampling.phone-with-usb.p1: This phone has the same Output when it plays through a USB DAC (Settings → Audio Devices → This phone → Output): the server makes the upsampled or DSD stream, and the app's USB driver plays it, DSD natively or as DoP.
upsampling.phone-with-usb.title: A phone with a USB DAC
upsampling.processor.p1: Upsampling and making DSD take far less of the processor than they did, with the same output: PCM as DSD256 takes 37% of one core per second of music where it took 68%, and upsampling ×16 runs 1.5 times as fast (measured on a 2.1 GHz Xeon). A track upsampled or made DSD as it plays gets the processor: playback keeps all the cores but one while it is made, or as many as Settings → Library Scanner → Processor → Cores for upsampling and DSD says (Auto, 1, 2 or 3). It is made some 30 seconds ahead of what the device has read, not flat out to its end.
upsampling.processor.title: The processor
upsampling.top.dd1: Original sends each track at its own rate. ×2 and ×4 upsample it (44.1 kHz to 88.2 or 176.4 kHz); Max goes to the highest rate the device takes in the track's family. Upsampling is made on the server in 64-bit float.
upsampling.top.dd10: Where a renderer has MPD beside it, as a Chord Poly does: Mandarin can hand MPD the queue, and MPD plays one track into the next by itself, as it plays its own library.
upsampling.top.dd11: An album's tracks go to the device as one stream, start to end, gapless however it joins files. A Mandarin Bridge is played one continuous stream anyway, and a Squeezelite player joins tracks from its own buffer.
upsampling.top.dd12: The volume is set on the device itself (its knob, or a line out on fixed), so Mandarin shows no slider and never scales the samples.
upsampling.top.dd13: ReplayGain for this device, to a target from −14 to −25 LUFS. Auto plays albums at album level and mixed tracks at track level.
upsampling.top.dd2: One filter for CD-rate sources and one for hi-res ones (or the same), each from the list: Standard (SoX's for PCM, Mandarin's own on the way to DSD), Gentle (rolls off earlier, rings for half as long), Gaussian (smooth, very short ringing, the top of a CD a little down), Gaussian steep (flat almost to 22 kHz, every sample of the file kept), Gaussian hi-res (for 88.2 kHz and up), and Long and Very long: the standard filter made 8 and 32 times as long, flat to 21.8 and 21.9 kHz for a CD and 270 and 284 dB down from 22.1 kHz, a track taking 0.15 and 0.6 s longer to start (Very long some 400 MB while it plays). Made as the track plays, and used for PCM as DSD too.
upsampling.top.dd3: For both filters. In minimum phase a filter keeps its levels at every frequency and puts its ringing after a sound (0.15 ms before it at most, where the linear filters ring 0.2 to 47 ms before). Gaussian steep keeps every sample of the file only in linear phase.
upsampling.top.dd4: Nothing goes above it, upsampled or not. Auto: as high as the device takes. ×16 (705.6 and 768 kHz) goes as WAV where the device takes WAV.
upsampling.top.dd5: The depth a converted or upsampled track is sent at: Auto is 24 (32-bit FLAC only where a device is set to 32). On Auto a 16-bit/44.1 kHz file plays as it is.
upsampling.top.dd6: Where Mandarin makes the PCM (upsampled, not made DSD): the bits the DAC resolves above its own noise, the dither put in at that bit, and how: Flat (the default), or Shaped of the 3rd or 5th order, its noise moved above the audio band (made at 88.2 kHz and up).
upsampling.top.dd7: For DSD sent to this device as PCM: take the DSD modulator's ultrasonic noise off above 50 or 30 kHz. Off keeps it, up to the top of the rate it goes at. DSD the device takes as DSD goes as it is.
upsampling.top.dd8: For a device that takes DSD: each track of the library that isn't DSD is made DSD as it plays and sent as a DSF, gapless from track to track. A 48 kHz-family track stays in its own family. The Output says how fast this server makes it, and whether that keeps up.
upsampling.top.dd9: How PCM is made DSD: the 7th order; the 7th order wide, which holds its noise down to 50 kHz (DSD128 and DSD256); or the 9th order, quieter in the audio band (DSD64 and DSD128).
upsampling.top.dt6: Real bits and Dither As sent · 23–20 · Flat · Shaped 3rd · Shaped 5th
upsampling.top.dt8: PCM as DSD Off · DSD64 · DSD128 · DSD256
upsampling.top.figcaption1: A Mandarin Bridge's Output in the Android app: Original, the highest rate on Auto, the bit depth on Auto, no DSD made, and fixed volume.
upsampling.top.p1: It opens with Sound, its settings as recipes: Bit-perfect; where the device takes more than 48 kHz, Upsampled with the Standard filter, with the Gaussian ones, with them in minimum phase, and with the Very long filter and shaped dither; where it takes DSD, DSD at its highest multiple with the 7th-order modulator. Each says what it does for that device, the one in use marked; a tap sets what it names. Custom, or any row changed, opens Advanced, every row of the Output below.

Versions are told by MusicBrainz's release group, else one act and one title with its version words off (2015 Remaster). The main is the highest resolution, or the one you choose with Make this the main version; the album's page lists every version with what tells it apart, a tap showing it in place. Features →
whats-new.before-v1-2.p3: The cover on top, the date, rate and length under it, the title across the page; then Tracks, Credits, About and Versions as tabs, centred, held at the top as the page scrolls with the page cut off cleanly under them. Share card is in ⋯. In the browser and the Android app.
whats-new.before-v1-2.p4: A track mastered to full scale clips between its samples when upsampled. Mandarin now counts every clipped sample and turns Now playing's line red; Headroom when upsampling (Auto) turns a track down by just what its true peak needs. Upsampling →
whats-new.before-v1-2.p5: The signal path says how fast a track is being made (Keeping up at 4.2× real time). An Output the server can't make in time, or the device can't play, is put back to the last one that played well, the track carrying on. Signal path →

whats-new.before-v1-3-0.li1: Removed: Playlists and Dynamic Playlists, with Qobuz's and Tidal's playlists and favourite tracks brought in as playlists (favourite albums still are).
whats-new.before-v1-3-0.li2: Fixed: plays, scrobbles and covers kept right through skips, drives mounted late and a DAC unplugged; a USB DAC pulled out of the phone pauses it, as headphones do; Mandarin Bridge 0.3.8.
whats-new.before-v1-3-0.li3: Improved: security, speed and reliability across the server, the page, the app and Mandarin Bridge. Releases are signed, and the server and Mandarin Bridge install only a signed update.
whats-new.before-v1-3-0.note1: Updating to v1.3.0: the server from Settings → Updates, the Android app beside it, each Mandarin Bridge from its own row. Every change is listed in the changelog.
whats-new.before-v1-3-0.p1: Mandarin v1.3.0, since v1.2.5, with Mandarin Bridge v0.3.8. An update following a code review: several under-the-hood fixes and improvements.
whats-new.before-v1-3-0.p2: Everything played, in every room, on a Mandarin Bridge or the phone, is scrobbled to your Last.fm account. Save your Last.fm key's shared secret beside the key in Settings → Setup → API Keys, tap Connect to Last.fm and allow Mandarin on Last.fm's page. Features →
whats-new.before-v1-3-0.p3: Overview, Discography and About, as an album's page has, with no links out to the web. Similar albums are your own library's alone, and genres are in English everywhere (Électronique is Electronic).

whats-new.before-v1-3-1.li1: Fixed: a large library's backup restores, where it was refused as “too large”.
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.li2: Fixed: while MusicBrainz is turning requests away, every lookup pauses (a minute, then longer, an hour at most), where it asked again every few seconds.
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.li3: Fixed: a Mandarin Bridge switched on in Settings → Audio Devices stays on, even while Qobuz's library is updated; a change the server refuses is said.
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.li4: Fixed: Mandarin Bridge 0.3.10 for Linux updates itself where systemd runs it, as on Mandarin OS.
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.li5: Fixed: the Android app pauses between tries when the server can't be reached, where it asked again and again.
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.li6: Changed: what Mandarin says to do (a forgotten password, an empty library, no rooms) fits how it is installed; on Mandarin OS, Shut down shuts the computer down too, and its power button starts it all again.
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.note1: Updating to v1.3.1: the server from Settings → Updates, the Android app beside it, each Mandarin Bridge from its own row. Mandarin OS updates itself from its system page; 0.1.3 and earlier reinstall 0.1.4 once (how). Every change is listed in the changelog.
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.p1: Mandarin v1.3.1, since v1.3.0, with Mandarin Bridge v0.3.10 and Mandarin OS 0.1.4. Mandarin OS arrives, the recommended way to run Mandarin, with Mandarin on Linux as the alternative; logs are always on and download as one file; and a handful of fixes.
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.p2: A lightweight operating system made only to run Mandarin Server, on a PC of its own, with its own system page (http://<box address>/) to watch over and look after everything: a shared folder for your music, USB drives mounted as they are plugged in, and a weekly upkeep when nothing plays. Installed from a USB stick made with balenaEtcher, a Linux terminal or EtchDroid on an Android phone. It updates itself in place, and goes back by itself to the version that worked if a new one doesn't start. The recommended way to run Mandarin. Mandarin OS →
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.p3: The alternative, for a Debian, Ubuntu or Raspberry Pi OS machine you already run (x64 or arm64): one line as root installs what Mandarin needs and runs it as a systemd service, its data in /var/lib/mandarin. Run again, it updates; --uninstall removes it. Install on Linux →
whats-new.before-v1-3-1.p4: The server, every Mandarin Bridge, the Android app and the page keep a log always, all of it on the server. Settings → Setup → Logs → Download all logs in a browser gives every log as one text file, in time order, each line saying where it came from; the app's Save log and Mandarin OS's system page do the same. Logs →

whats-new.changed.li1: The music folders are followed as they change: an album shows as it is copied in, a deletion within seconds, and a network share's or a mergerfs folder's changes within half a minute, where they waited for the six-hourly scan.
whats-new.changed.li2: Search's count (1 artist, 60+ albums) is under the search field, which keeps its width.
whats-new.changed.li3: Extended ends an edition's title, as Deluxe and Remastered do: Radical Optimism (Extended) is a version of Radical Optimism.

whats-new.fixed.li1: An album that mixes sample rates played nothing with Albums as one stream on, when its Output made DSD or upsampled to the highest rate.
whats-new.fixed.li2: An album deleted from the music folders stayed on its artist's page, in the app and the browser.
whats-new.fixed.li3: The Android app's album tabs were squashed into a column of letters, and the headings under them said the tabs again.
whats-new.fixed.li4: Mandarin Bridge's update said only SecureConnectionError when GitHub's certificate was refused; it now says why (a wrong clock, missing certificates).
whats-new.fixed.note1: Updating to v1.2.5: the server from Settings → Updates; the Android app beside it; each Mandarin Bridge from its own row. A reverse proxy on the server's machine needs TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1. Every change is listed in the changelog.

whats-new.lead: Mandarin v1.3.2, since v1.3.1, with Mandarin Bridge v0.3.10 and Mandarin OS 0.1.6. Mandarin OS 0.1.6, which keeps the box's settings when Mandarin is reinstalled; the Android app no longer ended by Android for its built-in Tailscale; and Mandarin OS's addresses given by the box's address.
whats-new.security.li1: Who sent a request is believed from forwarding headers only from the proxies named in TRUSTED_PROXIES and the built-in Tailscale. A reverse proxy on the same machine needs TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1. Configuration →
whats-new.security.li2: Covers from elsewhere are never fetched from the server's own machine or your network (but the Sonos speakers and hosts named in ART_HOSTS).
whats-new.security.li3: Addresses handed to speakers and players expire after 30 days, and a speaker asking without one gets only what it was handed.
whats-new.security.li4: Mandarin Bridge's port takes changes only as JSON, never from another site, and never updates backwards. A page on another port of the server's machine can't use your browser's sign-in either.
whats-new.security.li5: Scripts run only from Mandarin's own pages (a Content-Security-Policy).
whats-new.security.li6: With the sign-in off, only your own Tailscale devices count as home, not all of Tailscale's address range.
whats-new.security.li7: Releases can be signed, and the server's and the Linux Bridge's updates checked against Mandarin's release key.
whats-new.security.li8: Away from home, use Tailscale, never a port forward: the log now says when plain http arrives from outside. The workflows' actions are pinned, and a build that can be published needs the real signing key. Away from home →
whats-new.security.p1: A security audit of this version found fourteen things to put right; every one is fixed.
